headings.title: Introduction and Indications for Face Mask Oxygen Administration
headings.content: Oxygen administration via a face mask is a fundamental clinical skill required by nursing students in Nigeria and globally to manage patients experiencing acute or chronic hypoxemia. Oxygen is classified medically as a drug, which means it requires a physician's prescription specifying the flow rate and delivery method, except in emergency situations where prompt intervention is necessary to save a life. The primary indication for initiating face mask oxygen therapy is documented hypoxemia, which is typically identified when a patient's peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) falls below normal physiological parameters, usually under 92% to 94% on room air, or as otherwise directed by individualized patient care plans. Clinical manifestations that prompt the use of a face mask include acute respiratory distress, severe shortness of breath (dyspnea), tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis of the lips and nail beds, altered mental status resulting from cerebral hypoxia, and critical medical emergencies such as myocardial infarction, severe asthma exacerbations, carbon monoxide poisoning, and major trauma. Face masks are particularly useful over nasal cannulas when patients require higher concentrations of inspired oxygen (FiO2) or when they are mouth breathers. In Nigerian healthcare settings, nurses must recognize these critical indications promptly to prevent irreversible tissue hypoxia, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, and patient mortality. Understanding the underlying physiological need for supplemental oxygen ensures that nursing interventions are purposeful, evidence-based, and directly aligned with optimal patient outcomes in acute care environments.

headings.title: Equipment Needed for Oxygen Delivery via Face Mask
headings.content: Proper preparation and gathering of appropriate equipment are vital steps for ensuring the safe, efficient, and continuous administration of oxygen via a face mask. As a nursing student, you must systematically assemble all necessary supplies before initiating the procedure at the bedside. The essential equipment includes a reliable and verified oxygen source, which may be a central wall-outlet pipeline system equipped with a flowmeter or a portable compressed oxygen cylinder paired with a pressure regulator and flowmeter to control the volume of gas delivered in liters per minute (L/min). Additionally, a humidifier bottle filled with sterile water is required when delivering oxygen at higher flow rates or for extended periods to prevent drying and irritation of the patient's mucous membranes. You will also need an appropriate face mask of the correct size to ensure a snug, comfortable fit over the patient's nose and mouth, connecting oxygen tubing free of kinks or blockages, and a functioning pulse oximeter to continuously monitor oxygen saturation levels. Infection prevention supplies, such as hand hygiene products, and documentation materials are also integral parts of the setup. In resource-constrained Nigerian clinical environments, nurses must routinely inspect all regulators, flowmeters, and tubing for leaks or mechanical failures prior to patient attachment, thereby guaranteeing client safety and optimal equipment performance throughout the duration of the respiratory therapy.

headings.title: Types of Oxygen Face Masks and Flow Rates
headings.content: Different types of oxygen face masks are designed to deliver varying concentrations of inspired oxygen (FiO2) based on clinical requirements and specific flow rates. Simple face masks are commonly used for short-term oxygen therapy, typically delivering moderate FiO2 concentrations at flow rates ranging from 5 to 10 L/min, ensuring a minimum flow of 5 L/min to prevent the rebreathing of exhaled carbon dioxide trapped inside the mask. Partial rebreather masks feature a reservoir bag and one-way valves that allow the patient to breathe back a portion of their exhaled air, operating at flow rates of 6 to 15 L/min to maintain high oxygen concentrations. Non-rebreather masks are high-flow delivery systems equipped with multiple one-way valves that prevent room air entry and exhaled gas re-entry into the reservoir bag, capable of delivering FiO2 levels approaching 80% to 100% when driven by flow rates of 10 to 15 L/min, making them crucial for acute, severe hypoxia. Venturi masks represent a precise delivery system that utilizes interchangeable color-coded jets to mix specific amounts of room air with pure oxygen, delivering exact, constant FiO2 percentages regardless of the patient's respiratory pattern, which is especially vital for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients requiring controlled low-flow oxygen therapy. Nursing students must master these distinctions, flow rates, and FiO2 ranges to administer safe, accurate respiratory support suited to each patient's exact medical condition.

headings.title: Pre-Administration Assessment and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Before applying an oxygen face mask, comprehensive pre-administration assessment and meticulous patient preparation are essential nursing responsibilities. The nurse must begin by verifying the medical order for oxygen therapy, cross-checking the patient's identity, and assessing baseline respiratory status, which includes measuring respiratory rate, depth, pattern, chest excursion, lung auscultation findings, and recording baseline oxygen saturation via pulse oximetry. It is equally important to assess the patient's level of consciousness, skin color, and any signs of respiratory fatigue or distress. Preparation involves explaining the procedure to the patient and their family in a clear, reassuring manner to alleviate anxiety, as fear can exacerbate dyspnea and increase oxygen consumption. The nurse should inspect the patient's facial skin around the nose, mouth, and ears for any existing breakdown, pressure injuries, or irritation that might be worsened by a mask strap. Positioning the patient in a semi-Fowler's or high-Fowler's position is standard practice because this anatomical alignment maximizes lung expansion, lowers the diaphragm, and eases the work of breathing. Finally, ensure the patient's face is clean and free of excessive oils or secretions. In busy Nigerian hospital settings, taking these preparatory steps guarantees that oxygen therapy is both safe and well-tolerated by the patient, minimizing complications and improving overall therapeutic compliance.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Administering Oxygen
headings.content: Executing the step-by-step procedure for administering oxygen via a face mask requires clinical precision, adherence to infection control, and continuous patient communication. Begin by performing hand hygiene and donning clean gloves to maintain aseptic principles. Connect the oxygen tubing securely to the designated flowmeter on the wall outlet or oxygen cylinder, and attach the other end to the face mask. Turn on the oxygen source and adjust the flowmeter to the prescribed liters per minute (L/min), ensuring that gas is actively flowing through the tubing and out of the mask. For reservoir bag masks, ensure the bag fills properly before application. Gently apply the mask over the patient's nose and mouth, contouring the flexible metal strip over the bridge of the nose to minimize gaps. Secure the elastic strap comfortably around the back of the patient's head, ensuring it is neither too tight to cause pressure ulcers nor too loose to let the mask slip. Check that air is not blowing into the patient's eyes, which can cause severe irritation and dryness. Reassess the patient's comfort and verify that oxygen is successfully reaching the respiratory tract. Document the initiation of therapy, including the date, time, delivery device, flow rate, and baseline vital signs, maintaining accurate nursing records standard in Nigerian clinical practice.

headings.title: Ongoing Nursing Monitoring and Patient Safety
headings.content: Ongoing nursing monitoring and strict patient safety measures are critical components of high-quality oxygen therapy management. Once the face mask is in place, the nurse must continuously or intermittently assess the patient's respiratory rate, effort, breath sounds, skin color, and oxygen saturation using a pulse oximeter. Regular checks should be performed to ensure the prescribed flow rate remains accurate and that all tubing is free from kinks, twists, or disconnections. Safety is paramount because oxygen supports and accelerates combustion; therefore, strict 'No Smoking' and 'No Open Flames' policies must be enforced in the patient's room, and electrical equipment must be inspected for frayed wires or sparks. The nurse must routinely inspect the skin under the mask and elastic straps every two to four hours to check for signs of pressure breakdown, skin irritation, or moisture accumulation. Additionally, for patients with chronic respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the nurse must monitor for signs of carbon dioxide narcosis or decreased respiratory drive caused by excessive oxygen administration. Promptly reporting any sudden changes in clinical status to the attending physician ensures patient stability and prevents adverse respiratory complications across all healthcare settings in Nigeria.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Nursing Interventions
headings.content: Administering oxygen via a face mask carries potential complications that require vigilant nursing surveillance and prompt, skilled interventions. One major complication is oxygen toxicity, which occurs when high concentrations of inspired oxygen (FiO2 greater than 50%) are administered for an extended period, leading to alveolar-capillary membrane damage, pulmonary edema, and symptoms such as non-productive cough, substernal chest pain, and dyspnea. Another risk is mucous membrane drying and irritation, resulting from inadequate humidification, which can cause epistaxis, cracked lips, and thick, tenacious secretions that obstruct the airway. Skin breakdown and pressure ulcers frequently develop over the bridge of the nose, cheeks, and behind the ears from prolonged, tight mask contact. Furthermore, in patients with chronic hypercapnia, administration of high-flow oxygen can suppress the hypoxic respiratory drive, leading to carbon dioxide retention, somnolence, and respiratory arrest. Nursing interventions to mitigate these risks include ensuring proper humidification for flow rates above 4 L/min, applying protective barrier dressings to pressure points, rotating or removing the mask briefly during meals with alternative nasal cannula support if ordered, and carefully titrating oxygen to the lowest effective flow rate prescribed. By mastering these safety measures, nursing students in Nigeria ensure optimal patient protection and effective clinical management during oxygen therapy.
